items.title: 13.5 Reactions of the halogens with hydrogen

blocks.text: Halogens react with hydrogen to give hydrogen halides, H2 + X2 gives 2HX (X2 = F2, Cl2, Br2, I2); hydrogen halides are colourless gases that dissolve in water to form hydrohalic acids. The reactivity with hydrogen decreases from fluorine to iodine. Fluorine reacts explosively with hydrogen even at low temperature and in the dark, H2 + F2 gives 2HF, which dissolves in water as hydrofluoric acid. In UV light or with a spark chlorine reacts readily with hydrogen to give colourless HCl gas, which forms hydrochloric acid in water. Hydrogen bromide is produced when bromine reacts with hydrogen on heating, an exothermic reaction; HBr is less reactive than HCl and HF and forms strong hydrobromic acid in water. At high temperature with a catalyst iodine reacts with hydrogen to give hydrogen iodide, which forms hydroiodic acid in water; this reaction is reversible and very slow.
The reaction between H2 and F2 is explosive but that between H2 and I2 is slow and reversible. Explain.
